full_story_text:
Open the refrigerator, and you may see a small slider on the produce drawer.

It may look unimportant. But this slider changes how the drawer works.

Many refrigerators have two settings: low humidity and high humidity. The low-humidity setting lets more air move through the drawer. The high-humidity setting is closer to closed.

So, the drawer is not simply for “fruit” or “vegetables.” It has two different jobs.

One setting helps a gas leave. The other helps water stay.

As fruit ripens, it gives off a gas called ethylene. If other produce stays around too much of this gas, it may ripen too fast and spoil sooner. A ventilated, low-humidity drawer helps the gas move away.

Other foods lose water quickly. Their leaves or surfaces can become soft and wilted. A more closed, high-humidity drawer helps them keep moisture.

That is why using the right setting can help produce stay fresh longer. The important question is not only what the food is called. It is what kind of problem the food has.
point_one_text:
Sort by what the food needs
Ask two simple questions: Does this food give off a lot of ethylene? Will it wilt quickly? Apples and pears fit the first question, so low humidity is a useful choice. Leafy greens and broccoli fit the second, so high humidity is useful. The drawer works best when it matches the food’s weak point, not its supermarket label.
point_two_text:
Check the refrigerator first
Before choosing a setting, ask whether the food belongs in the refrigerator at all. Tomatoes and bananas are recommended for counter storage, so the low-humidity drawer is not a reason to chill them. ## Main Story

A refrigerator drawer can look like one simple box. But many drawers offer two settings: low humidity and high humidity.

In the low setting, more air can move through the drawer. In the high setting, the drawer is more closed, so moisture stays inside.

That small change gives fresh food a different place to stay. And it can help food stay fresh longer.

But the right choice is not simply “fruit here, vegetables there.”

Fresh food can lose quality in different ways. Some foods release ethylene, a natural gas that can make nearby produce ripen too quickly. Other foods lose water quickly and become soft or limp.

So the useful question is not only, “What kind of food is this?” It is also, “What problem is likely to happen first?”
point_one_text:
Sort by the problem, not the name
Here is a simple test. If the main worry is ethylene building up around the food, apples and pears fit the vented, low-humidity drawer. Air can help move the gas away.

If the main worry is water loss, leafy greens such as kale and vegetables such as broccoli fit the high-humidity drawer.

This is more useful than memorizing that all fruit belongs in one place and all vegetables belong in another.
point_two_text:
The slider is not the first question
Before choosing a setting, ask if the food belongs in the refrigerator. Bananas and tomatoes are recommended for the counter. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic need a cool, dry place.

Home advice is also not the same for every item. Commercial storage guidance lists 90–95% humidity for strawberries and oranges, but appliance makers do not agree on which home drawer to use. A precise number does not always give a precise household answer.
